questions.title: Header and footer
questions.text: Describe what is meant by a **header** and a **footer** in a document.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A header is an area in the top margin and a footer in the bottom margin of the page (1)
- whose content is repeated automatically on every page / of a section (1)
scheme.model_answer: A header is the area at the top margin and a footer the area at the bottom margin; whatever is written in them appears automatically on every page.

questions.title: Header vs heading
questions.text: A header and a heading are the same thing.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: A heading is a title inside the body text; a header is the repeated area in the top margin of every page.

questions.title: Items for headers and footers
questions.text: Select **two** items that are suitable for the header or footer of a project's technical documentation.

options.content: A screenshot of the login screen

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Version in the header
questions.text: Explain why the version number and date should be placed in the header of a requirements specification.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The document changes during the project / several versions exist (1)
- the version on every page shows readers whether they have the latest copy / pages from different versions are not mixed (1)

points.criterion: Reader can check it is current

scheme.model_answer: The specification is updated several times during the project, so showing the version and date on every page lets readers check they are using the latest version.

questions.title: Automatic page numbers
questions.text: Explain why page numbers should be inserted in the footer as a **field** rather than typed on each page.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The field updates automatically when pages are added / removed (1)
- saves time / no mistakes / consistent on every page (1)
scheme.model_answer: A page-number field updates itself when pages are added or deleted, so the numbers are always correct and do not need to be typed on every page.

questions.title: Header options
questions.text: Match each header/footer option to its use.

right.text: No header on the title page
Page numbers on the outside edge of a printed booklet
Each chapter shows its own title in the header

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R1, L2–R2, L3–R3. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Footnote
questions.text: Define the term **footnote**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A note at the bottom of the same page (1)
- linked to a reference mark / number in the text, giving a source or extra explanation (1)

points.criterion: Linked to a reference mark / purpose

scheme.model_answer: A note at the bottom of a page, linked by a superscript number in the text, that gives a source or extra explanation.

questions.title: Uses of footnotes
questions.text: State **two** uses of footnotes when documenting a project.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): cite / reference a source; explain a technical term or abbreviation; give extra detail / comment; cross-reference to another section / appendix
scheme.model_answer: 1 To give the source of information. 2 To explain a technical term.

questions.title: Footnote or endnote
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

prefill: Appears at the bottom of the same page as its reference
All notes are collected at the end of the document
The reader can see the note without turning pages

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Footnote (1); 2 Endnote (1); 3 Footnote (1)

questions.title: Why a footnote
questions.text: Explain why a writer might put the source of a statistic in a footnote rather than in brackets in the main text.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The main text is not interrupted / stays short and easy to read (1)
- the source is still on the same page and automatically numbered / avoids plagiarism (1)
scheme.model_answer: The sentence stays short and easy to read, while the source is still given at the bottom of the same page for readers who want to check it.

questions.title: Inserting a footnote
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

In Microsoft Word a footnote is inserted from the [[1]] tab. The small number in the main text that links to the footnote is called the reference [[2]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) References (2) mark

questions.title: Why use tables
questions.text: Explain why test results should be presented in a **table** in project documentation.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Each item (test data, expected and actual result) is in its own column / clearly organised (1)
- easy to read, compare expected and actual results, find failed tests (1)
scheme.model_answer: In a table the test data, expected result and actual result of each test are in separate columns, so they can be compared quickly and failed tests are easy to spot.

questions.title: Test-plan columns
questions.text: State **four** column headings that should be included in a test-plan table.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any four (1 each): test number; description / purpose; test data; type of test data (normal / extreme / erroneous); expected result; actual result; pass / fail / comments
scheme.model_answer: 1 Test data. 2 Type of test data. 3 Expected result. 4 Actual result.

questions.title: Table features
questions.text: Match each table feature to its purpose.

right.text: Shows the heading of each column
Gives the table a number and title, e.g. Table 3. Test plan
Makes one cell span several columns
Shows the column headings again on each new page

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R1, L2–R2, L3–R3, L4–R4. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Tables in documentation
questions.text: Complete the table with **two** column headings for each table used in project documentation.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Data dictionary (1): field name, data type, size, key, validation, description
Schedule (1): task, start date, end date, person responsible
Troubleshooting (1): problem / error message, cause, solution
scheme.model_answer: Data dictionary: field name, data type. Project schedule: task, deadline. Troubleshooting: error message, solution.
scheme.ai_instructions: Two suitable headings are needed for each mark.

questions.title: User guide contents
questions.text: Give **two** items that need to be included in the user guide for a new system.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): installation instructions / the steps required to install the product; details of backup procedures; required hardware and software; detailed instructions for each task; screenshots; error messages and troubleshooting; FAQ; contact details for support
scheme.model_answer: 1 Installation instructions. 2 How to deal with error messages.

questions.title: Improve a report
questions.text:
A student's 30-page project report has no page numbers, the test results are written as long paragraphs, and sources are written in brackets in the middle of sentences. The teacher cannot tell which version of the report is the newest.

Suggest how the student should improve the report using headers and footers, footnotes and tables. Justify each suggestion.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Up to 4 marks:
- Footer with automatic page numbers — readers find pages / sections (1)
- Header with title, version and date — teacher sees the latest version (1)
- Test results in a table with columns for data, expected, actual result — easy to compare (1)
- Sources moved into footnotes — text easier to read, sources still given (1)
scheme.model_answer: Add a footer with an automatic page-number field so the teacher can find each section; add a header with the report title, version and date so the newest version is obvious; present the test results in a table with columns for test data, expected result and actual result so they are easy to compare; and move the sources into footnotes so the sentences are easier to read while every source is still cited.

questions.title: A user guide page
questions.text:
The programmer provided the client with the **User guide 2026** for the new library system. A page is shown.

```text
+--------------------------------------------------+
| A:  User guide 2026 - Library System v1.3        |
+--------------------------------------------------+
|  4. Returning a book                             |
|  Scan the barcode on the back cover.(1)          |
|                                                  |
|  B:  (1) The barcode is on a white sticker.      |
+--------------------------------------------------+
| C:  (c) NIS Library            Page 4 of 18      |
+--------------------------------------------------+
```

scheme.mark_scheme: A Header (1); B Footnote (1); C Footer (1)
scheme.model_answer: A header; B footnote; C footer.

parts.title: User guide items
parts.text: Give **two** items that need to be included in the user guide.

scheme.mark_scheme: Installation instructions / steps to install (1); details of backup procedures (1); required hardware and software (1); detailed instructions for each function (1); troubleshooting (1) [Max 2]
scheme.model_answer: 1 Installation instructions. 2 Required hardware and software.

parts.title: Page numbers
parts.text: Explain why element C contains "Page 4 of 18".

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The user can find a section using the table of contents / knows where they are (1)
- can see if pages are missing; numbers update automatically (1)
scheme.model_answer: Readers can find sections listed in the contents and can see whether any of the 18 pages are missing.

parts.title: Version
parts.text: State why "v1.3" is shown in element A.

scheme.mark_scheme: To show the version of the guide / that it matches the current version of the system (1)
scheme.model_answer: It shows which version of the guide and system the page belongs to.

questions.title: Footnotes in a report
questions.text: A student writes the analysis section of her project report and wants to show where her information came from.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A note at the bottom of the page (1)
- linked to a reference mark in the text / gives source or explanation (1)
scheme.model_answer: A note at the bottom of the page linked to a number in the text, giving a source or explanation.

parts.title: Uses
parts.text: State **two** uses of footnotes in her report.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): cite sources; explain terms / abbreviations; extra details; cross-references
scheme.model_answer: 1 Citing the websites she used. 2 Explaining technical terms.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Footnotes appear at the bottom of the same page, endnotes at the end of the document / chapter (1)
- footnotes are quicker to read; endnotes suit long lists of references / keep pages clean (1)
scheme.model_answer: Footnotes are at the bottom of the same page, so they can be read immediately, whereas endnotes are collected at the end of the document, which suits long reference lists.

parts.title: Why footnotes
parts.text: Explain **one** advantage of using the word processor's footnote feature instead of typing notes at the bottom of each page.

scheme.mark_scheme: Advantage (1) + explanation (1): automatic numbering — renumbered when notes are added / moved; note stays on the same page as its reference when text moves; consistent formatting
scheme.model_answer: The notes are numbered automatically, so when she adds a new note in the middle, all the later notes are renumbered for her.

questions.title: Tables in documentation
questions.text: The programmer is writing the testing section of the technical documentation.

parts.title: Column headings
parts.text: State **four** column headings for the test-plan table.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any four (1 each): test number; description; test data; type of test data; expected result; actual result; pass / fail; comments
scheme.model_answer: Test number; test data; expected result; actual result.

parts.title: Good practice
parts.text: The table continues over three pages. State **two** ways to make it easy to read.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): repeat the header row on each page; numbered caption; bold / shaded header row; borders / banded rows; rows not split across pages; consistent alignment
scheme.model_answer: 1 Repeat the header row on every page. 2 Use banded (shaded) rows.

parts.title: Table vs paragraph
parts.text: Explain why a table is better than paragraphs of text for presenting the test results.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Each value has its own cell / organised in columns (1)
- expected and actual results can be compared quickly; failed tests found easily (1)
scheme.model_answer: In a table each test's data and results are in separate columns, so the expected and actual results can be compared at a glance.

summary: Using headers and footers, footnotes and tables when documenting a software project — what each is for, what it should contain, how to insert it in a word processor, and good practice for technical and user documentation.

blocks.content: Every software project produces **documentation**: the **requirements specification**, the **design**, the **test plan and results**, **technical documentation** for developers and a **user guide** for the people who will use the system. Good documents are **consistent, easy to navigate and easy to check**. Three word-processing features help with this: **headers and footers**, **footnotes** and **tables**.

+------------------------------------------------------+
| HEADER  Library System - User Guide v2.1    [logo]   |  <- repeated on every page
+------------------------------------------------------+
|                                                      |
|  3. Borrowing a book                                 |
|                                                      |
|  Scan the student card and then the book's barcode.¹ |  <- footnote reference mark
|                                                      |
|  +-----------+------------------+                    |
|  | Button    | Action           |                    |  <- table
|  +-----------+------------------+                    |
|  | Issue     | Lends the book   |                    |
|  | Return    | Records a return |                    |
|  +-----------+------------------+                    |
|  Table 2. Buttons on the Loans screen                |  <- caption
|  __________                                          |
|  ¹ Use the scanner on the left of the desk.          |  <- footnote text
+------------------------------------------------------+
| FOOTER  © NIS Library 2026            Page 7 of 24   |  <- repeated on every page
+------------------------------------------------------+
blocks.caption: The parts of a document page

blocks.title: Technical documentation vs user guide
rows: Algorithms, code listings, data dictionary, ERD, DFD, test plan, hardware/software requirements
Installation instructions, how to carry out tasks, screenshots, error messages and solutions, FAQ, backup procedures

blocks.content: A **header** is an area at the **top margin** of every page, and a **footer** an area at the **bottom margin**, whose content is **automatically repeated on every page** (or every page of a section) of the document.

blocks.title: What headers and footers usually contain
rows: The reader always knows which document a page belongs to
Helps the reader find their place
Shows whether the copy is up to date — vital for project documents that change
Navigation; matches the table of contents; shows if pages are missing
Who to contact about the document
Where the electronic file is stored

items.title: Advantages
items.content:
- Entered **once** and appear on **every page** automatically — saves time.
- **Consistent** layout across the whole document.
- **Fields** (page number, date, number of pages) update **automatically** when pages are added.
- Keep important information visible when pages are printed or separated.

items.title: Options in a word processor
items.content:
- **Different first page** — no header on the title page.
- **Different odd and even pages** — e.g. page numbers on the outside edge for a printed booklet.
- **Sections** — each chapter can have its own header text (e.g. the chapter title).
- Insert **fields**: page number, total pages, date, file name.

blocks.title: Inserting a header and footer (Microsoft Word / Google Docs)
items: **Insert → Header** (or double-click in the top margin) and type the document title and version.
**Insert → Footer**, then **Insert → Page number** (choose a format such as "Page X of Y").
Tick **Different first page** if the title page should have no header.
Close the header/footer area (double-click in the body text or press Esc).

blocks.content: A **note at the bottom of the same page**, linked to a **reference mark** (usually a superscript number¹) in the main text. It gives a **source, explanation or extra detail** without interrupting the main text.
Like a footnote, but all the notes are collected at the **end of the document** (or of a chapter) instead of at the bottom of each page.

items.title: What footnotes are used for in project documentation
items.content:
- **Citing sources** — the book, website or standard a fact comes from (avoids **plagiarism**).
- **Explaining a technical term** or abbreviation for a non-expert reader (e.g. "SQL — Structured Query Language").
- **Extra detail** that would break the flow of the main text (version numbers, exceptions, comments).
- **Cross-references** to another section, appendix or document.

items.title: Why use footnotes rather than brackets in the text
items.content:
- The main text stays **short and easy to read**.
- The note is on the **same page**, so the reader does not have to search for it.
- Numbering is **automatic** — notes are renumbered when text is added or moved.

blocks.title: Footnotes in a test report
blocks.content:
*All tests were run on the school's server¹ using the test data described in the test plan².*

---
¹ Windows Server 2022, 16 GB RAM, PostgreSQL 16.
² See Appendix B, Table 4.

blocks.title: Inserting a footnote
items: Place the cursor where the reference mark should go.
**References → Insert Footnote** (Word) / **Insert → Footnote** (Google Docs); shortcut **Ctrl + Alt + F** in Word.
Type the note at the bottom of the page.
To convert footnotes to endnotes: **References → Footnotes → Convert**.

blocks.title: Footnotes vs endnotes
rows: Quick — no need to turn pages
The reader must go to the end
Short explanations, sources the reader needs immediately
Long lists of references; documents with many notes

blocks.content: An arrangement of information in **rows and columns** of **cells**, used to present related data so that it is **easy to read, compare and find**.

blocks.title: Tables commonly used in project documentation
rows: Field name, data type, size, key, validation, description
Test no., description, test data, type of data, expected result, actual result
Task, start date, end date, person responsible

blocks.title: A test-plan table
blocks.content:
| Test no. | Description | Test data | Type | Expected result | Actual result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Valid age accepted | 15 | Normal | Accepted | Accepted ✔ |
| 2 | Lower boundary | 11 | Extreme | Accepted | Accepted ✔ |
| 3 | Out of range | 19 | Erroneous | Error message | Error message ✔ |
| 4 | Wrong type | "ten" | Erroneous | Error message | Program crashed ✘ |

items.title: Good practice for tables
items.content:
- A **header row** with clear column headings (bold, shaded); **repeat the header row** on each page if the table continues.
- A **caption** with a number and title ("Table 3. Test plan for the login form") so it can be referred to in the text.
- **Consistent** alignment: text left, numbers right or centred.
- Use **borders and shading** to make rows easy to follow; avoid too many colours.
- **Merge cells** for headings that span several columns; do not split a row across pages.
- Keep the table **simple** — one type of information per column.

items.title: Inserting and formatting a table
items.content:
- **Insert → Table**, choose the number of rows and columns.
- **Table Design / Layout** tabs: header row, banded rows, borders, merge and split cells, column width, alignment.
- **Repeat header rows** (Layout → Repeat Header Rows).
- **References → Insert Caption** to number the table automatically.
- **Insert → Table of Figures** creates a list of all tables in the document.

blocks.title: Why use a table instead of a paragraph?
rows: "Test 1 used 15, which is normal data; the expected result was accepted and it was accepted. Test 2 used 11, an extreme value…"
The same information in rows and columns — each value in its own cell, easy to **scan, compare and check**

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: A fragment of a page of the "User guide 2025" is shown. Name the element at the top of the page that contains the text "User guide 2025 — page 3". [1]**
**Header.**

**Q: Give two items that need to be included in the user guide. [2]**
**Installation instructions** / the steps required to install the product (1); details of **backup procedures** / required **hardware and software** / how to use each function / **troubleshooting** (1).

**Q: Explain why the programmer should use a footer with page numbers in the technical documentation. [2]**
The page numbers appear **automatically on every page** (1), so readers can **find sections from the table of contents** and notice if pages are **missing** (1).

**Q: Explain one reason for using footnotes in a project report. [2]**
To **cite the source** of information (1) without interrupting the main text, so the report is easy to read and avoids **plagiarism** (1).

**Q: Explain why the test results should be presented in a table. [2]**
Each test's data, expected and actual result are in **separate columns** (1), so they are **easy to compare** and failed tests can be found quickly (1).

- Typing the page number by hand on each page instead of inserting a **page-number field**.
- Confusing a **header** (top margin, repeated) with a **heading** (a title in the body text).
- Using footnotes for **main** information — they are for sources and extra detail.
- Tables without **column headings** or **captions**.
- Putting different kinds of data in the same column.
